reviews.author: Byung-Hoon Lee (Cool Guy)
reviews.text:
Central Asia Street is a street in Gwanghui-dong, Jung-gu, Seoul, South Korea.
It was given this name because the region has a relative concentration of Central Asian-themed companies.

This street was created as early as the 1980s, starting with the establishment of diplomatic relations between Korea and the Soviet Union in 1990, as foreigners from the former Soviet Union gathered together, and the majority were people from Russia, Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Buryatia. Bundle merchants and fabric dealers came here for trading at the nearby Dongdaemun Market, with accommodations and facilities. He opened a currency exchange office and established a base.

It boomed in 1997 thanks to the low exchange rate due to the IMF foreign exchange crisis, and Russian traders and Uzbek and Mongolian migrant workers fluent in Russian flocked to the area. However, when Russia faced a moratorium in 1998, many Russians withdrew, and only Central Asian workers remained, opening shops and restaurants, and it became what it is today.
In 2022, a themed street creation project was carried out under the leadership of Jung-gu Office, and floors and notices with traditional carpet patterns were installed.

reviews.text:
# A place worth visiting by chance

This is the new gate of Hanyangdoseong, located not far from Heunginjimun. This is the gate through which Japanese envoys came and went, and it is also called Sugumun Gate as the stream of Namsan flows nearby. The dingy fortress stones, weathered by time, gave off an old-fashioned feel. The door is always open.

Also, because it was the gate through which the corpse exited, it was often called Sigu Gate. It is said that since burials within the city walls were not allowed in principle, the corpses of the people were taken out through this gate. It is an aside that only kings were allowed to have a funeral procession through the main gate. For this reason, there were many cemeteries outside the gate, and it is said that it later became Shindang-dong, where shamans lived.

It is also known as the gate through which King Injo fled to go to Namhansanseong Fortress during the Manchu War. It could be said that they were so tense that they had no time to worry about the desperate situation of the Qing army. I tried to imagine how the king must have felt in the unprecedented situation of passing through the Sigumun Gate.

This is a memorial statue to commemorate Jeon Tae-il (22 years old), a tailor at the sewing factory in Pyeonghwa Market, who set himself on fire in front of Pyeonghwa Market in Seoul on November 13, 1970, while protesting against poor working conditions and demanding compliance with the Labor Standards Act. In 2005, the city of Seoul created Jeon Tae-il Street in the area near Pyeonghwa Market on Cheonggyecheon-ro and installed a statue and bronze plaque commemorating Jeon Tae-il within the Cheonggyecheon Beodeul Bridge. In 2013, the area around the site of Jeon Tae-il’s self-immolation (on the main road between Buildings A and B of Pyeonghwa Market in Sindang-dong) was selected as a ‘Seoul City Future Heritage’. The basis for selection is that it is a place with high preservation value as a place where the lives of workers, who were forced to make one-sided sacrifices in the process of high growth and suffered, emerged as a social problem and a historical event that became a signal for Korea's labor movement and democratization movement.

reviews.author: Choi Jong Oh

Dongdaemun. Heunginjimun is the eastern gate of Hanyangdoseong during the Joseon Dynasty, and is often called Dongdaemun.
Heunginjimun is the only one of the four main gates of Hanyangdoseong that has a semicircular fortress to protect it.
It was first built in the 5th year of King Taejo's reign (1396) in the Joseon Dynasty, and the current building was rebuilt in the 6th year of King Gojong's reign (1869).
The roof is a trapezoid-shaped hipped roof when viewed from the front, and is a two-story building with 5 rooms on the front and 2 rooms on the sides.
Heunginjimun is evaluated as a building that well demonstrates the characteristics of the architectural style of the late Joseon Dynasty.

It was discovered during demolition of Dongdaemun Stadium. Now that the Ogansumun of Cheonggyecheon has disappeared, it is the only watermung in Hanyangdoseong that retains its old appearance. It is a facility for discharging domestic sewage and the Namsomundongcheon Stream, which originates from Namsan, and is a core relic of Hanyangdoseong that was excavated.

It is an Igansumun because there are two channels through which water flows out. It is said that since it was a vulnerable point for defense, a wooden fence/iron fence was installed and operated with defense personnel as shown in the photo. The grooves inside the water bowl appear to be where a fence was placed.

When I looked up close, each stone was huge. It was much bigger than Sungnyemun Gate, and I was surprised how they moved it. The stones laid on the floor are called sheet stones and are said to be used to prevent the ground from sinking due to being washed away by water.

reviews.author: Productive Minho
reviews.text:
This is the water gate of Hanyangdoseong that crosses Cheonggyecheon. It was demolished during the Japanese colonial period because it obstructed the flow of water, so it does not remain anymore. It was called Ogansumun because it had five arch-shaped water tunnels, and Ogansu Bridge is currently located at this location. There is a sculpture of Ogansumun on the embankment next to the bridge, but it is a bit poor.

There is a legend that Im Keok-jeong's group escaped from Ogansumun Gate. It is said that the area under the water gate was vulnerable to defense, so even though a barbed wire fence was installed, it was often used as a stealth route by thieves and robbers. During restoration, old iron bars were discovered.

The square stone on the bridge represents the Ogansumun foundation stone discovered during the restoration project. Due to traffic flow issues, it could not be restored like in the case of Gwangtong Bridge and Igan Water Gate. If it had been there, it would have added a touch of modern charm to Cheonggyecheon, but it was a shame!

In November 1930, Gyeongseong Suburban Track Co., Ltd. acquired a railway license for a 4.3km section from Wangsimni to Ttukseom and laid a narrow-gauge railway.
However, due to management difficulties, the license was transferred to Gyeongseong Track Co., Ltd.
From April 1932, Gyeongseong Tramway Co., Ltd. took over and operated the Gyeongseong Tramway, and in October of that year, the route was expanded and a separate line was built between Dongdaemun and Wangsimni. The terminal station and the company were near Heunginjimun (Dongdaemun) (current location of Dongdaemun Tourist Hotel). In 1934, a new branch line of approximately 7.2 km from Sanghuwon Station to Gwangjang-ri was constructed.
At the time, the Gyeongseong Railroad was an important means of transportation transporting passengers and goods within Seoul, but a significant portion of the railroad was destroyed during the Korean War. As a result, the operation of the railroad was taken over by the Seoul Metropolitan Government and was discontinued in 1963.

*incident and accident*
On the afternoon of June 18, 1936, a train carrying 96 third-year students at Gyeongseong Normal School left Dongdaemun Station and headed to the training site in Ttukseom when it collided with a freight train of the same Gyeongseong Track Company at Yongdu Bridge, causing many injuries.
The cause of the accident was determined to be because the car was old and its brakes were broken.
Also, one of the causes of the accident was that the capacity was 62 people, but the speed was high due to the weight of the 96 people on board.
Choi Gyeong-sik, who was the driver at the time, was sentenced to 10 months in prison.
Due to this incident, the Gyeongseong Track Company suffered a huge blow, losing 500 won and tarnishing its image.
This became a big issue at the time and was on people's lips.

reviews.text: Gakjaseongseok, records of fortifications carved into stones: When walking along the walls of Hanyangdoseong Fortress, you will often find stones with letters engraved on them. These stones, called Gakjaseongseok (刻字城石), are traces of the history of the Hanyangdoseong Fortress. To date, 288 engraved stone stones have been discovered throughout the entire section of Hanyangdoseong (as of 2015), showing different characteristics depending on when the walls were built. In addition, the records engraved on the stone are consistent with various national literary records of the Joseon Dynasty, making it an important resource that provides a glimpse into not only the construction period of each section of the Hanyangdoseong but also the thoroughness of the city's management.

The Dongdaemun Stadium Memorial Hall displays various materials related to Dongdaemun Stadium, which was used as a cradle of Korean sports and a venue for public events and commemorative events for over 80 years from its construction during the Japanese colonial period in 1925 until its demolition in 2007.

reviews.text:
If DDP's unconventional design points to the future, this place sheds light on the past. The ruins of Hanyangdoseong and buildings from the Joseon Dynasty were discovered where Dongdaemun Stadium disappeared, and were reborn as a park with an image that is at odds with DDP.

Igansumun Gate, which was discovered rather than destroyed, is one of the impressive sights. The curved concrete facility reminiscent of a stadium and the two lighting towers seem to symbolize the past Dongdaemun Stadium. I was able to learn more about the history by visiting the history museum and playground memorial hall in the park.

It was disappointing that the proportion of exhibitions at Dongdaemun Stadium, which was the birthplace of domestic sports, was small. I understand the historical remains exhibition hall, but I thought it would be more appropriate if the site near the gallery door was used as a playground to reminisce on memories and as a sports facility for residents. I think it would have been nice to have placed the old stands in the empty concrete facility!
